extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Victorian humour; readers of Dickens' comic character sketches
extracted.subtask_description: Short, humorous character sketches (vignettes) lampooning social types — couples defined by a dominant comic trait (the plausible couple, the egotistical couple, etc.). The page models how to portray types through amplified particulars, dialogue, and anecdote.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE PLAUSIBLE COUPLE
rubrics_metrics.description: A couple whose chief talent is pleasing the world by adapting themselves to its tastes; always 'delightful', 'affectionate', 'good-hearted'—they find merit everywhere and profess frankness while practising social flattery and strategic depreciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics and behaviours illustrated: play into each other's hands to maximize social success; use pet names and mutual fondness as performance; praise absent people only so the praise reflects upon someone present; depreciate others in ways that flatter present persons; contrive invitations and introductions (the Clickits anecdote) to bind social circles; speak 'their minds' while actually manipulating impressions. Anti-pattern: their seeming candour conceals calculated flattery and self-advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE NICE LITTLE COUPLE
rubrics_metrics.description: A tiny, sprightly couple exemplified by Mr. and Mrs. Chirrup: Mrs. Chirrup is 'the prettiest of all little women', an incomparable housewife and expert carver; Mr. Chirrup is fond, proud, and jocose — together they are neat, well-matched, and wholly agreeable in company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques and details used to create comic effect: pack many pleasing domestic virtues into small physical description (condensation of virtues); emphasise minute, charming particulars (neat foot, soft voice, precise carving technique); stage convivial scenes (dinner, round game, supper tray) to show social harmony; use a recurring bachelor friend to produce light banter and matrimonial contrast. Moral note: the sketch treats smallness as concentrated virtue and delights in domestic minutiae.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE EGOTISTICAL COUPLE
rubrics_metrics.description: Couples dominated by egotism in two principal ways: (1) both spouses are self-centered and claim universal experience and acquaintance with great events/people; (2) each spouse egotistically magnifies the other's merits (mutual adulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical comic devices: hyperbolic claims to knowing or being connected to famous incidents/people (e.g., involvement in historical anecdotes), repetitive narrative monopolising conversation, competing reminiscences and unreliable memory, and a tendency to turn every topic toward themselves (health, diet, personal trials). The worst form is deliberate, ostentatious egotism that seeks many hearers. Examples supplied: a couple asserting they 'have been everything but dead' and Mr. and Mrs. Sliverstone who stage-manage each other's sacrifices and labours. Anti-pattern: such behaviour sours listeners and provokes disgust rather than pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE COUPLE WHO CODDLE THEMSELVES
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypochondriacal, over-protective couple (with an enabling relative) who treat every change of weather, slight ailment, or discomfort as a crisis; take elaborate preventive measures (flannel, hot water, chamomile, camphor), ritualise care, and centre domestic life on symptoms and remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic particulars used: specific accoutrements (wash-leather socks, India-rubber shoes, hare-skin under-waistcoat), theatrical departure ritual, detailed ministrations on return (rubbing feet until the subject grimaces), measured dosing (carbonate of soda weighed with scales), and nightly 'tittivating' and composing draughts. Scenes alternate between fuss and ordinary domestic pleasures (good dinners, carving) to emphasize the absurdity. The author generalises that such couples are selfish, slothful, and predisposed to charge external causes for self-inflicted ills.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE OLD COUPLE
rubrics_metrics.description: An elderly married pair whose bodies and memories are worn by time: bent figures, grey hair, tottering step, whose wedding joys have receded into a long catalogue of cares, griefs, and losses (dead children, faded bridal garments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrayal relies on poignant particulars and nostalgic contrast: preservation of a few bridal dresses, faded whiteness, weakened memories of youthful companions, and the slow accumulation of sorrow. The sketch uses restrained, reflective tone to elicit pathos rather than direct mockery, showing how time transforms vivacity into gentle decay and recollection into dreamlike fragments.
